newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Bulgaria-type crisis unlikely in Romania - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria-type crisis unlikely in Romania - analysts.

text.p: Unlike neighbouring Bulgaria, Romania has avoided economic crisis but analysts say the country's new centrist government must carry out tough reforms to put the economy on track.

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea's renewed commitment to put together a tight reform package is encouraging, the analysts said. It is being drafted with help from International Monetary Fund and World Bank experts.

During a televised news conference late on Thursday, which he shared with World Bank and European Union representatives, Ciorbea told fellow Romanians that reforms were their only chance to avoid the plight of their Bulgarian neighbours.

Analysts say that the IMF is keen to avoid a repeat of the crisis in Bulgaria, where inflation has soared to 50 percent a month and the lev has gone into a freefall, with protesters out in the streets demanding early elections.
"Romania isn't in the same situation as Bulgaria," Mark Holdsworth of ING Barings in London told Reuters on Friday.
"The situation is very different because there's a real realisation by the IMF that the situation in Bulgaria mustn't be repeated," he said.

Fund negotiators, backed by World Bank experts, have been in Bucharest for two weeks working with the centrist goverment on a reform package to underpin the resumption of credits withheld or suspended for Romania.
The outlook is quite different for Bulgaria, where the IMF has said it was prepared to resume funding talks as soon as a new government is in place.
"We feel confident that the IMF and the Romanian government are both working towards the same goal, which is achieving macro-economic stability," Holdsworth said.

Analysts say that last month's visit to Bucharest by IMF chief Michel Camdessus was meant to signal the Fund's support for the reformists who pushed leftists out of office in general elections last November.

"His very presence is an indication of the seriousness with which the IMF takes the Romanian reform process," Holdsworth said. "Romanian politics has reached new maturity following the November elections and reforms are crucial."
"(Romania's) medium-term prospects are good, but they are totally conditional on the government producing its reform package," he said.

Ciorbea, whose government relies on an absolute majority from a centrist coalition in parliament, said on Thursday that the reform package, expected to include foreign exchange market liberalisation, would be made public within two weeks.
He predicted negative growth for 1997 but made no specific forecasts for the coming year.

Romanian inflation climbed to 57 percent last year -- more than triple the target agreed with the IMF -- and the state budget gap is believed to have bulged to 5.7 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP) against a 2.2 percent forecast.

Despite its woes -- due to slow reforms under the former leftists -- Romania does not face the debt servicing problems saddling Bulgaria, whose President Petar Stoyanov has said that his country could default on a $10 billion foreign debt.

"The two situations are quite different. Romania's foreign debt is very low as a percentage of the GDP or exports and it cannot be compared to Bulgaria," Parvoleta Shtereva, a debt analyst with ING Barings told Reuters from London.
In 1996 Romania borrowed around $1.4 billion from world markets and serviced debt payments of around $1.2 billion. The country's medium- and long-term foreign debt stands at $6.9 billion.
